rituals.name: TWO-FEELING SPLIT
rituals.plain:
Two feelings can share a day. They don't need a custody battle.
If there is fear about fear, anger about sadness, etc., place the first feeling left and reaction-to-feeling right.
Don't decide which is correct.
Hold both.

Don't rehearse the words after judging them.

rituals.name: NAME-LETTER BIAS
rituals.plain:
Do your own initials feel oddly likeable? Your name has a tiny fan club.
Pick two letters from your name and two common letters not in it. Rank the four by simple liking before analysing why.
Judge the letters themselves, not words they form.
Don't choose initials only if that makes the effect too obvious.

rituals.name: GAZE CHORUS

A crowd of imagined eyes can point different ways. You aren't always the main attraction.
Picture three neutral observers. First make all three look at the same object. Then scatter their gaze toward three different places and compare where attention is pulled.
Observer identities and positions stay fixed.
Don't change facial expressions.

rituals.name: JOINT-ATTENTION TRIANGLE
rituals.plain:
What are two people actually looking at? Less mind-reading, more geometry.
Picture Alex, Ben and three objects: a cup, book and lamp. Alex is looking at the cup; Ben is pointing at the cup. Find the shared target without inventing either person's thoughts.
Use only visible gaze/pointing direction.
Keep the people mentally separate from the object they both orient toward.

rituals.name: COMMON-KNOWLEDGE LADDER
rituals.plain:
What do you know they know? No infinite mind-reading staircase.
Take a simple fact such as 'the meeting moved to 3pm.' Mark: I know it; they know it; I know that they know it. Stop at the highest level actually supported.
Use one concrete fact only.
Don't fill unsupported levels with assumptions.

Repeat once with the eyes looking right.

rituals.name: IMPLICATURE GAP
rituals.plain:
What was said, and what did you add? Subtitles aren't always official.
Use: 'Some of the reports are finished.' Literal: at least some are finished. Implied: not all are finished. Notice that the implication is not identical to the sentence.
Write one literal meaning and one inferred meaning.
Don't treat the inferred meaning as a quoted fact.

rituals.name: ONE HELP LINE
rituals.plain:
SUPPORT FIRST
ONE HELP LINE

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Form one sentence saying you are struggling and need someone with you or helping you verify things.

NEXT
Say/send if needed.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Help-seeking becomes executable.

REMEMBER
You do not need perfect words before connection can start.

SAFETY
This should lower the barrier to contact, not replace contact; if safety is uncertain, send or say the help sentence to a real person now rather than rehearsing it privately.

NEXT

Safety improves through environment.

Moving toward a staffed safer environment changes the real risk landscape.

SAFETY
This only works if you actually move toward a safer staffed environment; do not remain alone in a risky setting while mentally imagining the route.

SUPPORT FIRST
DECISION SLOWDOWN

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Pause major irreversible decisions until activation is lower or support is present.

NEXT
Immediate safety actions are exempt.

WHY THIS MATTERS
High activation stops driving irreversible choices alone.

REMEMBER
Extreme activation is a poor time for nonurgent high-stakes commitments.

SAFETY
This applies to nonurgent high-stakes choices during extreme activation; it must never delay emergency action, medical care, or an immediate step needed to keep someone safe.

rituals.name: PRINTED-FACT ANCHOR
rituals.plain:
SUPPORT FIRST
PRINTED-FACT ANCHOR

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Read one stable external fact aloud or silently—such as a device clock, room sign, address, date display or printed label—and recheck the exact same fact once.

NEXT
If you still feel unable to verify what is happening, involve another person or professional support.

WHY THIS MATTERS
One present fact is anchored to an external source that can be checked again.

REMEMBER
Printed or physically displayed words provide a reference that can be rechecked by more than one person.

SAFETY
This is a shared-reality aid, not proof that everything is fine; if frightening uncertainty persists, show the same external information to a trusted person or clinician instead of checking it alone repeatedly.

rituals.name: EXTERNAL ONLY MODE
rituals.plain:
SUPPORT FIRST
EXTERNAL ONLY MODE

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Use visible objects, clocks, messages, known people, and direct conversation as decision inputs.

NEXT
No decoding unusual perceptions.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Decision-making shifts toward verifiable information.

REMEMBER
During destabilising uncertainty, externally checkable facts can temporarily outrank private interpretation.

SAFETY
This is temporary support for destabilising uncertainty; rely on checkable external facts and human verification, and do not use inner interpretation to override clear safety information.

rituals.name: CO-REGULATION CALL
rituals.plain:
SUPPORT FIRST
CO-REGULATION CALL

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Call, sit with, or message someone and tell them you need company or steadiness.

NEXT
No performance required.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Regulation becomes shared rather than solitary.

REMEMBER
Another person’s steady presence can be the intervention itself.

SAFETY
This requires an actual safe person when activation is high; if the call does not increase safety or you cannot stay safe, escalate to appropriate crisis, medical, or emergency support.

SUPPORT FIRST
SAFE COMPANION

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Have someone you trust stay nearby while you slow decisions and get support.

NEXT
Let them help with practical safety.

WHY THIS MATTERS
High activation is held with another human present.

REMEMBER
Support becomes stronger when it turns from an idea into shared time and presence.

SAFETY
This means staying with a trustworthy person, not merely messaging once; if risk is acute, avoid being left alone until appropriate support has taken over.

rituals.name: KEYS-WALLET-PHONE
rituals.plain:
SUPPORT FIRST
KEYS-WALLET-PHONE

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Place keys/cards/phone or other action-enabling items in the care of a trusted person or out of immediate reach.

NEXT
Explain why.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Impulsive options become harder to execute.

REMEMBER
Temporarily limiting access to keys, money or other risky means changes what can happen next.

SAFETY
This is about reducing access to high-impact actions; hand over or secure only items that can be managed safely, and involve a trusted person if judgment or impulse control is significantly impaired.

[USER THOUGHT]

NEXT

Assessment responsibility moves to qualified support.

Confusing or high-risk symptoms become safer when assessment responsibility passes to an appropriate professional.

SAFETY
This means ending self-interpretation once symptoms are confusing or high-risk; give the relevant facts to a qualified professional and follow real-world assessment rather than continuing rituals.

rituals.name: REMOVE FROM CUE
rituals.plain:
SUPPORT FIRST
REMOVE FROM CUE

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Physically step away from gambling/drug/alcohol/weapon/other high-risk cue when applicable and seek support.

NEXT
Do not negotiate at cue.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Cue-action proximity decreases.

REMEMBER
Leaving a setting strongly linked to risky behaviour removes part of the cue system itself.

SAFETY
This requires real distance from the high-risk environment; do not linger near the cue to prove you can resist it, and bring in support if leaving safely is difficult.

rituals.name: TRUSTED CHECKLIST
rituals.plain:
SUPPORT FIRST
TRUSTED CHECKLIST

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Take the next listed safe step—person, place, service, medication instructions, etc.

NEXT
No new plan required.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Action is guided by a stable external plan.

REMEMBER
A safety plan written during a steadier state preserves earlier judgment for use when thinking is under pressure.

SAFETY
This should be a prewritten, credible safety plan; if the plan no longer fits the level of risk, escalate beyond the checklist instead of repeating it mechanically.

SUPPORT FIRST
WAIT WITH SOMEONE

[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Stay alongside someone you trust for a defined period before acting on frightening or impulsive conclusions.

NEXT
Discuss facts, not certainty loops.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Time and company reduce pressure for immediate action.

REMEMBER
Letting nonurgent time pass in company changes both isolation and decision pressure.

SAFETY
This is supervised delay for nonurgent action; choose a genuinely safe companion and do not use waiting to postpone emergency care or another time-critical safety step.

rituals.name: EMERGENCY THRESHOLD

SUPPORT FIRST
EMERGENCY THRESHOLD

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
If there is immediate danger, inability to stay safe, severe medical symptoms, or risk to others, contact emergency services.

NEXT
No app game first.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Escalation is triggered by clear safety conditions.

REMEMBER
Clear emergency conditions remove the need to debate whether to seek urgent help in the worst moment.

SAFETY
This is for acting on predefined red flags, not debating them after they occur; when the threshold is met, contact the appropriate emergency service or urgent support.

rituals.name: MEDICATION REALITY CHECK
rituals.plain:
SUPPORT FIRST
MEDICATION REALITY CHECK

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
If medication may be involved in unusual symptoms or missed doses, contact prescriber/pharmacist/medical service.

NEXT
Follow their guidance.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Medication decisions remain clinical.

REMEMBER
Medication dosing belongs with clinicians and pharmacists because safe changes depend on information an app cannot assess.

SAFETY
This keeps dosing decisions with clinicians or pharmacists; do not start, stop, double, skip, or otherwise change prescribed medication because of a ritual or moment of confusion.

rituals.name: WITHDRAWAL SUPPORT
rituals.plain:
SUPPORT FIRST
WITHDRAWAL SUPPORT

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Contact urgent medical care when withdrawal could be dangerous.

NEXT
Stay with support if possible.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Risk is managed through medical support rather than willpower.

REMEMBER
Severe withdrawal can involve medical danger that inward coping cannot evaluate or treat.

SAFETY
This treats possible severe withdrawal as a medical issue; seizures, severe confusion, marked agitation, hallucination-like experiences, or other serious symptoms require urgent professional assessment rather than self-guided coping.

rituals.name: TWO-SOURCE AGREEMENT
rituals.plain:
SUPPORT FIRST
TWO-SOURCE AGREEMENT

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Choose one safe present detail—for example, current time or location. Check it on one external source, then confirm it with a second source or trusted person.

NEXT
If the sources disagree or you still feel unsafe, stop the game and seek human/professional support.

WHY THIS MATTERS
One reality anchor is supported by two independently checkable sources.

REMEMBER
When two genuinely independent sources converge on the same present fact, agreement becomes a stronger safety check than repeated reporting from one information stream.

SAFETY
This only counts when the sources are genuinely independent and reliable; if the fact affects immediate safety, use a qualified person or service rather than endlessly collecting more confirmations.

rituals.name: SAFE CONTACT TREE
rituals.plain:
SUPPORT FIRST
SAFE CONTACT TREE

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Try contact 1; if unavailable, contact 2; then service 3.

NEXT
Stop once connected.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Help-seeking has a defined fallback path.

REMEMBER
A preselected contact hierarchy turns help-seeking into the next available connection rather than a fresh decision under stress.

SAFETY
This should move you to the next available real person without repeated indecision; if nobody on the list is reachable and risk is rising, escalate to crisis, medical, or emergency support.

rituals.name: STAY VISIBLE
rituals.plain:
SUPPORT FIRST
STAY VISIBLE

WHAT'S HAPPENING
[USER THOUGHT]

DO NOW
Remain with trusted people or in an appropriate staffed place until support takes over.

NEXT
No solo test.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Isolation risk decreases through visibility and contact.

REMEMBER
Remaining visible and connected during acute risk changes the conditions around dangerous action.

SAFETY
This means avoiding isolation during acute risk; remain with trusted people or in an appropriate staffed place and do not leave to test whether you can manage the danger alone.
